kurals.tamil:
படைகுடி கூழ்அமைச்சு நட்பரண் ஆறும்
உடையான் அரசருள் ஏறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Padai kudi koozh amaichu natparan aarum
Udaiyaan arasarul eru.
kurals.meaning: A ruler who possesses all six parts of a state — an army, a loyal people, resources, wise ministers, allies, and strong fortifications — stands among kings like a lion among beasts.
kurals.elementary: Think of a strong table that needs all its legs to stand. A kingdom needs six “legs”: soldiers, happy people, food and money, good helpers, friends, and strong walls. A king who has all six is like the lion — the strongest of all the kings.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the Book of Polity not with the king’s personality but with a structural inventory of the state: padai (army), kudi (citizenry), koozh (food/revenue), amaichu (ministry), natpu (alliances), and aran (fortification). This six-limbed model closely parallels the saptanga (“seven-limbed”) theory of the state found in Kautilya’s Arthashastra, minus the king himself — who in the Kural is the one who ‘possesses’ the six, making him the integrating seventh element. The image of the ‘eru’ (a male lion or bull, the pre-eminent male of its kind) frames kingship as excellence in a competitive field of rulers rather than divine right. The chapter structure of the Porutpaal then follows this list, with later chapters devoted to each limb (army, fortress, friendship, ministers), so this kural functions as a table of contents for the whole book of statecraft.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya lists the constituent elements of sovereignty as the king, the minister, the country, the fort, the treasury, the army, and the ally (Arthashastra 6.1, the saptanga theory).
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya’s classic Indian theory says a state is made of seven parts that must all be healthy for the kingdom to survive.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s six possessions of a great king are almost exactly Kautilya’s list once the king himself is set aside.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close structural parallel; paraphrased because the Book 6 wording was not verified verbatim online.

christianity.quote_or_event: “In the multitude of people is the king’s honour: but in the want of people is the destruction of the prince.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs says a king’s glory depends on having many people under him; without them his rule collapses.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s ‘kudi’ (the people) as a core limb of royal greatness, though it names only one of the six elements.
christianity._accuracy_note: Partial match — covers the ‘people’ element only, not the full six-part model.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an instructs the community to prepare whatever strength and war-horses it can muster so that enemies are deterred (Qur’an 8:60).
islam.explanation: Muslims are told to be ready with military strength so that enemies think twice about attacking.
islam.tie_back: Parallels the ‘padai’ (army) and ‘aran’ (defence) limbs of the Kural’s strong state.
islam._accuracy_note: Covers only the military/defence elements; no single Islamic text lists all six.

judaism.quote_or_event: Solomon’s reign is described with an organised cabinet of officials (1 Kings 4:1-7), district officers supplying provisions (4:7, 4:22-23), vast stables of horses and chariots (4:26), and a treaty of friendship with Hiram of Tyre (5:12).
judaism.explanation: The Bible pictures Solomon’s kingdom as great because it had ministers, food supplies, an army, and allies all at once.
judaism.tie_back: Solomon’s kingdom is a narrative illustration of nearly every limb the Kural names: ministers, provisions, army, and alliance.
judaism._accuracy_note: Narrative parallel covering most of the six elements; not a stated doctrine.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) is said to possess seven ‘treasures’, including the elephant and horse treasures (military might), the householder treasure (wealth), and the counsellor treasure (wise minister) (e.g. Mahasudassana Sutta, DN 17).
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist texts imagine the ideal world-ruler as owning seven special treasures that make his rule complete.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it defines the supreme king by a checklist of possessions — army, wealth, and counsel among them.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Similar ‘list of royal assets’ form; the specific items only partially overlap (jewel and queen treasures have no Kural equivalent).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Hesiod’s account, Zeus wins and keeps his kingship over the gods only by gathering allies — the Cyclopes who forge his thunderbolt and the Hundred-Handed ones who fight beside him against the Titans.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even Zeus needed weapons, fighters, and friends to become and stay king of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural’s point that a ruler’s supremacy rests on army and allies, not on personal power alone.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Mythic illustration of the army and alliance limbs only.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “First, there must be food; secondly, arts, for life requires many instruments; thirdly, there must be arms … fourthly, there must be a certain amount of revenue, both for internal needs, and for the purposes of war; fifthly, or rather first, there must be a care of religion … sixthly, and most necessary of all …”
philosophy.explanation: Setting out what a state cannot exist without, Aristotle lists six requisites, among them food, arms, revenue and, last and most necessary, a power of deciding what is just and expedient among citizens.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s six limbs of the state, Aristotle’s list gives six things a polity must have, including the army and the treasury, though the two lists differ item by item.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Politics, Book VII, ch. 8 (1328b) (tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett, Book VII). Striking six-fold structure with overlaps (arms/army, revenue/resources); Aristotle's arts, religion and judiciary do not match the Kural's ministers, allies and forts, and there is no lion simile. The sixth item is summarised in the explanation, not quoted.

kurals.tamil:
அஞ்சாமை ஈகை அறிவூக்கம் இந்நான்கும்
எஞ்சாமை வேந்தர்க் கியல்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Anjaamai eegai arivookkam innaankum
Enjaamai vendhark kiyalbu.
kurals.meaning: Fearlessness, generosity, wisdom, and energetic drive — never to be lacking in these four is the true nature of a king.
kurals.elementary: A good team captain is brave, shares with everyone, knows what to do, and never gets lazy. This kural says a real king must have all four of these — and never run out of any of them.
kurals.university: Having described the external assets of the state, Valluvar now names the four inner qualities of the ruler: anjaamai (fearlessness), eegai (liberality), arivu (wisdom), and ookkam (energy or zeal). The key word is enjaamai — ‘without deficiency’ — which makes the standard one of constancy: a king who is brave in one crisis but timid in the next, or generous only when convenient, does not meet it. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar pair the qualities functionally: courage and energy to act, wisdom to decide rightly, and generosity to bind people to the ruler. The list resembles the Bhagavad Gita’s catalogue of kshatriya traits and Plato’s requirements for the philosopher-ruler, suggesting a widely shared intuition that rulership needs both a warrior’s nerve and a sage’s judgment.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Heroism, power, determination, resourcefulness, courage in battle, generosity and leadership are the natural qualities of work for the kṣatriyas.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the natural qualities of the warrior-ruler class: bravery, strength, firmness, skill, generosity, and the ability to lead.
hinduism.tie_back: Heroism and courage match anjaamai, generosity matches eegai, and determination/resourcefulness match ookkam and arivu.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match — nearly all four Kural virtues appear in the Gita’s list of royal-warrior traits.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD;”
christianity.explanation: Isaiah describes the coming ideal king, whom Christians identify with Christ, as filled with wisdom, good counsel, and strength.
christianity.tie_back: Wisdom and might together echo the Kural’s pairing of arivu with courage and energy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Covers wisdom and strength; generosity is not named.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and has increased him abundantly in knowledge and stature.”
islam.explanation: When the Israelites doubted Talut (Saul) as king because he was not rich, their prophet replied that God had given him more knowledge and strength.
islam.tie_back: Kingship is justified by wisdom and physical/moral strength — two of the Kural’s four royal qualities.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear match for wisdom and courage/strength; generosity and energy not addressed.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.”
judaism.explanation: God tells Joshua, the new leader of Israel, to be strong and fearless as he takes command.
judaism.tie_back: Echoes anjaamai — fearlessness as the first requirement of leadership.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The ‘ten royal virtues’ (dasa raja dhamma) listed in the Jataka tradition begin with dana (generosity) and include sila (morality), pariccaga (self-sacrifice), and tapa (self-discipline/energy).
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist stories give kings a list of ten virtues, starting with generosity.
buddhism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s idea of a fixed set of royal virtues with generosity central, though Buddhist lists stress gentleness over fearlessness.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Overlaps on generosity and discipline; emphasis differs (non-anger, non-violence).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sarpedon tells Glaucus that kings are honoured with the best seats, meat, and lands only because they must fight in the front ranks; privilege is earned by courage.
greek_mythology.explanation: A Trojan-allied prince explains that kings get special honours only because they are the bravest in battle.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Links royal standing to fearlessness, just as the Kural makes anjaamai a permanent kingly trait.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; covers courage only, with an implicit link to royal generosity/honour.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato has Socrates list the natural gifts required in the philosopher who would rule: good memory, quickness to learn, magnificence (greatness of spirit), graciousness, and kinship with truth, justice, courage, and temperance.
philosophy.explanation: Plato says the ideal ruler must be quick-minded, big-hearted, and brave.
philosophy.tie_back: Wisdom, greatness of spirit, and courage correspond to arivu, eegai, and anjaamai.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a genuine list of ruler-qualities with substantial overlap.

kurals.tamil:
தூங்காமை கல்வி துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றும்
நீங்கா நிலனான் பவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Thoongaamai kalvi thunivudaimai immoondrum
Neengaa nilanaan bavarkku.
kurals.meaning: Alertness that never delays, learning, and firm resolve — these three must never leave those who rule a land.
kurals.elementary: A good lifeguard never falls asleep on duty, knows how to swim and rescue, and jumps in bravely when needed. A ruler needs the same three things: stay awake, keep learning, and be brave enough to act.
kurals.university: Thoongaamai literally means ‘not sleeping’, and the commentators read it as freedom from sloth and delay — prompt action when action is due. Kalvi (learning) and thunivu (decisive courage) complete the triad, and the verb neengaa (‘must not depart’) again stresses that these are permanent dispositions, not occasional performances. The combination is significant: learning without resolve produces a hesitant ruler, and resolve without learning produces a reckless one, while both fail without vigilance. Kautilya’s Arthashastra makes the same point in its timetable for the king, which divides the day and night into tasks and insists that the king ‘shall ever be wakeful’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “IF a king is energetic, his subjects will be equally energetic. If he is reckless, they will not only be reckless likewise, but also eat into his works. Besides, a reckless king will easily fall into the hands of his enemies. Hence the king shall ever be wakeful.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya says the people copy the king’s energy or laziness, so the king must always stay alert.
hinduism.tie_back: “Ever be wakeful” is almost a literal rendering of the Kural’s thoongaamai (sleeplessness/vigilance).
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very strong match on vigilance; learning and courage are addressed elsewhere in Book 1.

christianity.quote_or_event: “...he that giveth, let him do it with simplicity; he that ruleth, with diligence; he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the church that whoever has the gift of leading must lead diligently, not lazily.
christianity.tie_back: Diligence in ruling parallels thoongaamai — the ruler’s refusal to be slothful.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that the strong believer is better and more beloved to God than the weak one, and urged believers to strive eagerly for what benefits them, seek God’s help, and not give in to helplessness (Sahih Muslim 2664).
islam.explanation: Muslims are told to be strong and keen, and never to give up or become passive.
islam.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s pairing of unflagging effort with firm resolve.
islam._accuracy_note: General teaching for all believers, not specific to rulers; translations vary so paraphrased.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them:”
judaism.explanation: The Torah requires Israel’s king to write his own copy of the law and study it every day of his life.
judaism.tie_back: Makes lifelong learning (kalvi) a legal duty of kingship, as the Kural makes it a quality that must never leave the ruler.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match for the learning element; vigilance and courage not addressed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “I am never content with exerting myself or with despatching business. Truly, I consider the welfare of all to be my duty, and the root of this is exertion and the prompt despatch of business.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist emperor Ashoka says he never stops working hard and dealing quickly with the business of state, because the welfare of all depends on it.
buddhism.tie_back: “Prompt despatch of business” is exactly the no-delay alertness that thoongaamai demands.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Rock Edict VI (tr. S. Dhammika)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on vigilance and energy from an actual Buddhist ruler.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “To sleep the whole night through beseemeth not a man that is a counsellor, to whom a host is entrusted, and upon whom rest so many cares.”
greek_mythology.explanation: A dream sent by Zeus scolds King Agamemnon: a leader responsible for an army should not sleep all night.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A near-literal statement of thoongaamai — a ruler must not ‘sleep’ on his responsibilities.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Excellent match for vigilance (ironically delivered by a deceptive dream).

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy, and political greatness and wisdom meet in one... cities will never have rest from their evils.”
philosophy.explanation: Plato argues that cities will suffer until rulers become truly learned and wise.
philosophy.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s insistence that kalvi (learning) must never depart from those who rule.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches learning; vigilance and resolve not addressed.

kurals.tamil:
அறனிழுக்கா தல்லவை நீக்கி மறனிழுக்கா
மானம் உடைய தரசு.
kurals.transliteration:
Aranizhukkaa thallavai neekki maranizhukkaa
Maanam udaiya tharasu.
kurals.meaning: True kingship never swerves from righteousness, removes whatever is unrighteous from the land, and holds to an honour that never falls short in courage.
kurals.elementary: A good referee always follows the rules, sends off players who cheat, and is brave enough to make hard calls. This kural says a real ruler is like that: always fair, stops wrongdoing, and never loses courage or self-respect.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a pair of parallel negatives: aran izhukkaa (not slipping from dharma) and maran izhukkaa (not slipping from martial valour), bound together by maanam — honour or self-respect. Between them sits the positive duty allavai neekki, ‘removing what is not right’, which commentators read both as the king avoiding vice himself and as his suppressing wrongdoing in the realm. The effect is to insist that courage and justice must travel together: valour without righteousness becomes tyranny, while righteousness without valour cannot protect anyone. This coupling of justice and courage has a close analogue in Cicero’s claim that greatness of spirit divorced from justice is a vice rather than a virtue.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If the king did not, without tiring, inflict punishment on those worthy to be punished, the stronger would roast the weaker, like fish on a spit;”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu say that if the king fails to punish wrongdoers, the strong will destroy the weak.
hinduism.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s ‘allavai neekki’ — the king’s duty to remove unrighteousness from the land.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the removal-of-wrong clause; the honour/valour element is not in this verse.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Take away the wicked from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs says a king’s rule becomes secure when wicked people are removed from his presence.
christianity.tie_back: Directly parallels ‘allavai neekki’ — removing the unrighteous so that rule rests on justice.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match for justice and removal of wrong; courage not mentioned.

islam.quote_or_event: “O David, indeed We have made you a successor upon the earth, so judge between the people in truth and do not follow [your own] desire, as it will lead you astray from the way of Allah.”
islam.explanation: God tells King David to rule with truth and not follow his own wishes.
islam.tie_back: Matches ‘aran izhukkaa’ — a ruler who never slips from righteousness.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on justice and self-restraint; courage/honour not explicit.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thus saith the LORD; Execute ye judgment and righteousness, and deliver the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor: and do no wrong, do no violence to the stranger, the fatherless, nor the widow...”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah tells the king of Judah to do justice, rescue the oppressed, and never do wrong himself.
judaism.tie_back: Combines the Kural’s two duties: staying righteous oneself and actively removing oppression.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on righteousness and removing wrong; valour element absent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that when kings are unrighteous, their ministers, officials, and people become unrighteous too, and even nature falls out of order; when kings are righteous, righteousness spreads downward through the whole realm (AN 4.70).
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a king’s goodness or badness flows down to everyone in the kingdom.
buddhism.tie_back: Explains why the Kural requires the king to never slip from dharma — his conduct sets the moral tone of the land.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; matches the righteousness element, not courage/honour.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On his way to Athens, the young Theseus deliberately takes the dangerous land route and kills a series of bandits (Sinis, Sciron, Procrustes and others) who preyed on travellers, before becoming king.
greek_mythology.explanation: Theseus bravely clears the road of robbers and murderers, making it safe for everyone, and later becomes a respected king.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows courage harnessed to justice — removing wrongdoers — which is the Kural’s joining of maram with aram.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Mythic illustration of courageous removal of evil; honour theme implicit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero argues that the loftiness of spirit shown in danger and toil, if it lacks justice and fights for selfish ends rather than the common good, is a vice rather than a virtue.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero says bravery is only good when it serves justice; bravery for selfish ends is actually bad.
philosophy.tie_back: Mirrors the Kural’s insistence that valour (maram) and righteousness (aram) must both remain unbroken together.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong conceptual match on joining courage to justice.

kurals.tamil:
இயற்றலும் ஈட்டலுங் காத்தலும் காத்த
வகுத்தலும் வல்ல தரசு.
kurals.transliteration:
Iyatralum eettalung kaaththalum kaaththa
Vaguththalum valla tharasu.
kurals.meaning: A true government is one skilled in creating sources of wealth, gathering it in, safeguarding it, and then distributing what has been safeguarded wisely.
kurals.elementary: Think of a farmer who plants seeds, harvests the crop, stores it safely in a barn, and then shares it out so everyone has food all year. A good ruler does the same with the country’s wealth: make it, collect it, protect it, and share it fairly.
kurals.university: This is the Kural’s compact theory of public finance, expressed as four verbs: iyatral (generating new sources of revenue), eettal (collecting), kaaththal (guarding), and vaguththal (apportioning or allocating). The sequence is cyclical — well-allocated spending produces the prosperity from which new revenue is generated — and it treats wealth as a means of governance rather than a royal possession. Commentators note that vaguththal implies planned allocation among competing ends (defence, welfare, religious and civic works), not merely generosity. The same logic appears in Kalidasa’s praise of King Dilipa, who taxed his people only as the sun draws up water, in order to return it a thousandfold as rain.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kalidasa says King Dilipa collected taxes from his subjects only for their own welfare, just as the sun draws up moisture only to return it a thousandfold as rain.
hinduism.explanation: A famous Sanskrit poem compares a good king to the sun, which takes water from the earth only to give it back as much more rain.
hinduism.tie_back: Captures the Kural’s full cycle: gathering wealth (eettal) only in order to distribute it wisely (vaguththal).
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; very close in spirit to the collect-and-distribute cycle.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the Lord said, Who then is that faithful and wise steward, whom his lord shall make ruler over his household, to give them their portion of meat in due season?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus praises the wise manager who distributes food to the household at the right time.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the guarding (kaaththal) and timely distribution (vaguththal) of resources.
christianity._accuracy_note: Parable about stewardship rather than kingship proper; covers two of four verbs.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Joseph] said, ‘Appoint me over the storehouses of the land. Indeed, I will be a knowing guardian.’”
islam.explanation: Prophet Joseph asks the king of Egypt to put him in charge of the nation’s storehouses, promising to guard them wisely.
islam.tie_back: ‘Knowing guardian’ of the storehouses is precisely the Kural’s kaaththal (safeguarding) joined to wise management.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match for storing and guarding; Joseph is minister, not king.

judaism.quote_or_event: Joseph advises Pharaoh to collect a fifth of the harvest during seven years of plenty, store it in the cities under guard, and distribute it during the seven years of famine (Genesis 41:34-36, 41:47-57).
judaism.explanation: Joseph saves Egypt by collecting grain in good years, keeping it safe, and handing it out during the famine.
judaism.tie_back: Enacts all of the Kural’s stages — gathering, storing, guarding, and distributing wealth.
judaism._accuracy_note: Narrative match to the full cycle; administrator rather than monarch.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kutadanta Sutta, a king troubled by banditry is advised not to raise taxes or punish, but to give seed and fodder to farmers, capital to traders, and wages to officials; the country then prospers and the treasury fills.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells of a king who fixed crime and poverty by investing in farmers, merchants, and workers, which made the whole kingdom richer.
buddhism.tie_back: Illustrates iyatral — generating new sources of wealth — and wise allocation (vaguththal).
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong match for creating and allocating wealth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas wishes that everything he touches turn to gold, and nearly starves because his wealth cannot be used; he begs Dionysus to undo the gift.
greek_mythology.explanation: A king who only wanted to pile up gold found that wealth that cannot be used is worthless.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A cautionary contrast: acquisition without right use fails, whereas the Kural demands that gathered wealth be distributed.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Contrast rather than parallel; no close Greek-myth analogue for royal finance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The Aristotelian Oeconomica holds that the manager of a household or estate must be able to acquire wealth, to preserve it, and to make proper use of it.
philosophy.explanation: An ancient Greek treatise on management says good managers must know how to earn, keep, and use wealth.
philosophy.tie_back: Nearly the same sequence of competences as the Kural’s generate-gather-guard-distribute.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; authorship disputed (Aristotelian school); household rather than state.

kurals.tamil:
காட்சிக் கெளியன் கடுஞ்சொல்லன் அல்லனேல்
மீக்கூறும் மன்னன் நிலம்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaatchik keliyan kadunjollan allanel
Meekkoorum mannan nilam.
kurals.meaning: If a king is easy for his people to approach and is not harsh in speech, the whole world will praise his land.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a school principal whose door is always open and who speaks kindly to every student. Everyone would say that’s a great school! A king who is easy to meet and never speaks rudely makes his whole country admired.
kurals.university: Kaatchikku eliyan — ‘easy to be seen’ — names the political virtue of accessibility: a ruler who can be reached by ordinary petitioners without layers of gatekeepers. The second condition, not being kadunjollan (a speaker of harsh words), concerns the manner of the encounter once access is granted. The reward is striking: it is the land (nilam), not merely the king, that the world exalts, implying that a ruler’s approachability shapes the reputation of the whole polity. Kautilya warns in almost identical terms that a king who makes himself inaccessible breeds confusion and public disaffection, and Islamic tradition records a hadith threatening divine seclusion from the ruler who secludes himself from his people.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When in the court, he shall never cause his petitioners to wait at the door, for when a king makes himself inaccessible to his people and entrusts his work to his immediate officers, he may be sure to engender confusion in business, and to cause thereby public disaffection, and himself a prey to his enemies.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya warns that a king who keeps people waiting and hides behind officials will make his people unhappy and his kingdom weak.
hinduism.tie_back: The exact virtue of ‘kaatchikku eliyan’ — being easy for subjects to reach.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match for accessibility; harsh speech not addressed here.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus invites everyone who is tired or burdened to come to him, describing himself as gentle and humble.
christianity.tie_back: Christ as king is openly approachable and gentle — both halves of the Kural’s ideal.
christianity._accuracy_note: Spiritual rather than political kingship, but matches accessibility and gentleness.

islam.quote_or_event: “If Allah puts anyone in the position of authority over the affairs of the Muslims, and he secludes himself (from them), not fulfilling their needs, wants, and poverty, Allah will keep Himself away from him, not fulfilling his need, want and poverty.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warned that a ruler who hides from his people and ignores their needs will find God hiding from him.
islam.tie_back: A direct religious sanction for the Kural’s demand that a ruler be easy to approach.
islam._accuracy_note: Very strong match on accessibility of rulers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; but ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment is God’s:”
judaism.explanation: Moses instructs Israel’s judges to listen to ordinary people just as carefully as to important ones.
judaism.tie_back: Hearing ‘the small as well as the great’ is the practical meaning of a ruler being easy to approach.
judaism._accuracy_note: Addressed to judges under Moses; matches accessibility, not speech.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “...at any time, whether I am eating, in the women’s quarters, the bed chamber, the chariot, the palanquin, in the park or wherever, reporters are to be posted with instructions to report to me the affairs of the people so that I might attend to these affairs wherever I am.”
buddhism.explanation: Emperor Ashoka ordered that the people’s concerns be brought to him at any hour, wherever he was.
buddhism.tie_back: An actual Buddhist king institutionalising the Kural’s ideal of being always reachable.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Rock Edict VI (tr. S. Dhammika)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the opening of Sophocles’ Oedipus the King, Oedipus comes out in person to the suppliants at his palace, saying he did not think it right to hear of their troubles from messengers but came himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: King Oedipus goes out to meet his suffering people personally instead of sending servants.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Dramatises the approachable king the Kural praises — though the play then shows his temper toward Teiresias and Creon.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; accessibility matches, but Oedipus is later harsh in speech.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A readiness to listen to those who had anything to propose for the common weal … He was also easy in conversation, and he made himself agreeable without any offensive affectation … There was in him nothing harsh, nor implacable, nor violent.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius describes his adoptive father, the emperor Antoninus Pius, as a ruler who listened to anyone with something useful to propose, was easy to talk to, and had nothing harsh about him.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s praiseworthy king drawn from life: easy to approach and never harsh in speech.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book I, §16 (tr. George Long)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Long, Book I); excerpts joined with ellipses from the long §16 portrait. Strong match on accessibility and absence of harshness; the Kural's result (the world praising his land) is not stated here.

kurals.tamil:
இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க வல்லார்க்குத் தன்சொலால்
தான்கண் டனைத்திவ் வுலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Insolaal eeththalikka vallaarkkuth thansolaal
Thaankan danaiththiv vulagu.
kurals.meaning: For the ruler who can give with kind words and protect those who come to him, the world becomes just as he wishes it to be, praising him and following his word.
kurals.elementary: When a friend shares their snacks and says something nice while doing it, everyone wants to be on their team. A king who gives generously, speaks kindly, and protects people finds that the whole world is happy to follow him.
kurals.university: The kural joins three verbs — speaking sweetly (insol), giving (eeththal), and protecting (alittal) — and makes their combination the source of consent. The second line is compressed: ‘the world becomes as he sees it by his word’, which commentators such as Parimelazhagar read as the world both praising him and conforming to his intentions. The insight is that legitimacy is earned through the manner as well as the substance of benefaction: gifts given with contempt create resentment, whereas gifts with kind words create loyalty. This closely matches the Buddhist ‘bases of fellowship’ (generosity, kind speech, beneficial help, consistency) and the counsel Rehoboam’s elders gave him — ‘speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Valmiki describes Rama as one who always spoke gently, was the first to speak and greet others kindly, and was devoted to the welfare of his people, which is why the citizens longed for him to be crowned (Ayodhya Kanda 1-2).
hinduism.explanation: Rama was loved by everyone because he spoke kindly first and cared for the people, so they wanted him to be king.
hinduism.tie_back: Sweet speech plus care for the people wins the world’s consent — the Kural’s formula for a ruler whom all follow.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Rama’s described character; not a doctrinal statement.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Many will intreat the favour of the prince: and every man is a friend to him that giveth gifts.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs notes that people seek the favour of a generous ruler and befriend those who give.
christianity.tie_back: Generosity (eeththal) draws people to the ruler, as the Kural says the world follows the giving king.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches generosity; somewhat cynical tone, and kind speech not mentioned.

islam.quote_or_event: “So by mercy from Allah, [O Muhammad], you were lenient with them. And if you had been rude [in speech] and harsh in heart, they would have disbanded from about you.”
islam.explanation: God tells the Prophet that his gentleness kept his followers close; if he had been harsh they would have left.
islam.tie_back: The same logic as the Kural: gentle speech is what keeps people gathered around a leader.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on kind speech producing loyalty; giving not mentioned in this verse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If thou wilt be a servant unto this people this day, and wilt serve them, and answer them, and speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever.”
judaism.explanation: The old advisers tell King Rehoboam that if he serves the people and speaks kindly, they will serve him forever. He ignores them and loses most of the kingdom.
judaism.tie_back: Almost a restatement of the Kural: good words and service make the people follow the ruler’s will.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near-direct parallel, reinforced by the negative outcome of Rehoboam’s harshness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There are these four grounds for the bonds of fellowship. Which four? Generosity, kind words, beneficial help, consistency.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names four things that hold people together: giving, kind speech, helping, and treating people consistently.
buddhism.tie_back: Generosity, kind words, and beneficial help map precisely onto the Kural’s giving, sweet speech, and protection.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on three elements; addressed to all, traditionally applied to rulers.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...for therefore are there princes wise in heart, because when the people are being misguided in their assembly, they set right the matter again with ease, persuading them with gentle words.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says the Muses give good kings the gift of gentle, persuasive speech, which lets them guide their people.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A king who wins people by gentle words finds them following his word — the Kural’s second line.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on kind speech and consent; generosity absent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is not easy to say how far an affable and courteous manner in conversation may go toward winning the affections.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero tells his son that a courteous, kindly manner of speech wins people over in ways that are hard to measure, and points to letters from Philip, Antipater and Antigonus urging their heirs to win the people with kind words.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the ruler who gives with kind words finds the world following him, though Cicero stresses gracious speech more than giving and protection.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book II, §48 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (De Officiis II.44-89, Miller); the quote begins mid-sentence ('...and yet, it is not easy to say...'), with an editorial capital 'I'. Partial match: covers kind words winning affection, but not the Kural's pairing with generosity and protection of those who come to the ruler. The content of the royal letters is summarised from the surrounding passage.

kurals.tamil:
முறைசெய்து காப்பாற்றும் மன்னவன் மக்கட்கு
இறையென்று வைக்கப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Muraiseydhu kaappaatrum mannavan makkatku
Iraiyendru vaikkap padum.
kurals.meaning: The king who rules with justice and protects his people will be regarded by them as a god.
kurals.elementary: When a lifeguard keeps everyone safe and is always fair, the swimmers look up to them like a hero. This kural says a ruler who is fair and protects everyone is looked up to by the people almost like God.
kurals.university: The word irai carries a deliberate double meaning — both ‘lord/king’ and ‘God’ — and the chapter title Iraimaatchi itself plays on it. Crucially, Valluvar makes divinity conditional: the king is ‘placed’ (vaikkappadum) as god by the people only because he does murai (justice, due order) and protects them. This inverts the claim of inherent divine kingship found in texts like the Laws of Manu, grounding sacral status in performance rather than birth. Aristotle’s remark that a person of pre-eminent virtue ‘may truly be deemed a God among men’ and Psalm 82’s address to judges as ‘gods’ who must defend the poor show the same conditional logic.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Even an infant king must not be despised, (from an idea) that he is a (mere) mortal; for he is a great deity in human form.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu say that the king, even a child king, is a god in human form and must be respected.
hinduism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s king-as-god image, but Manu makes divinity inherent, while the Kural makes it earned by justice and protection.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Same image with an instructive difference in its grounds.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For he is the minister of God to thee for good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that a ruler who punishes wrong and protects the good is acting as God’s servant.
christianity.tie_back: The ruler who does justice stands in God’s place for the people, close to the Kural’s claim.
christianity._accuracy_note: Ruler as God’s agent rather than as god; conditional on doing good.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet listed a just ruler first among the seven whom God will shade on the Day when there is no shade but His (Sahih al-Bukhari 660).
islam.explanation: Islam teaches that a just ruler will receive God’s special protection on Judgment Day.
islam.tie_back: A just, protecting ruler holds a uniquely exalted status — though Islam strictly denies any divinity to humans.
islam._accuracy_note: Exaltation of the just ruler, but explicitly not deification.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.”
judaism.explanation: In Psalm 82, God calls the rulers and judges ‘gods’, but only after demanding that they ‘defend the poor and fatherless’ — and warns that the unjust among them will die like men.
judaism.tie_back: Rulers are called ‘gods’ precisely in their role of doing justice and protecting the weak, as in the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual match, including the conditional nature of the title.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Agganna Sutta, the first king is called Mahasammata, ‘the Great Elect’, chosen by the people to judge and punish wrongdoers in return for a share of rice (DN 27).
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist texts say the first king was simply chosen by the people to keep order, not sent by the gods.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it grounds kingship in doing justice for the people — but it deliberately denies the king divine status.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Honest partial match: same justice-based legitimacy, opposite view on divinity.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And when he passes through a gathering, they greet him as a god with gentle reverence, and he is conspicuous amongst the assembled.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says a king who judges fairly is greeted by the people like a god.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural: the just king is ‘placed as god’ by his people.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: reverence as a god earned by just judgement.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Such an one may truly be deemed a God among men.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says a person whose virtue far surpasses everyone else’s would be like a god among humans and should rule.
philosophy.tie_back: Divine regard grounded in pre-eminent virtue — the same conditional deification as the Kural.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match; Aristotle speaks of outstanding virtue generally, not only justice.

kurals.tamil:
செவிகைப்பச் சொற்பொறுக்கும் பண்புடை வேந்தன்
கவிகைக்கீழ்த் தங்கும் உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Sevikaippach sorporukkum panbudai vendhan
Kavigaikkeezhth thangum ulagu.
kurals.meaning: The whole world will shelter beneath the royal umbrella of a king gracious enough to bear words that are bitter to his ears.
kurals.elementary: Good medicine often tastes bad, but it makes you better. A wise king listens even when someone tells him an unpleasant truth. Because of that, everyone feels safe living under his rule.
kurals.university: Sevi kaippa — ‘so that the ear tastes bitterness’ — is a vivid synaesthetic image for criticism that is unpleasant to hear. The commentators specify that these are the admonitions of wise elders and ministers, whose duty (developed in the later chapter on ‘Seeking the Help of the Great’) is to rebuke the king when needed. The kavigai (royal parasol) is the symbol of sovereign protection, so the kural’s claim is that tolerance of criticism is not a weakness but the condition under which the whole world will rest securely under the ruler’s shade. Vidura’s warning in the Mahabharata that speakers and hearers of unpleasant but healing words are rare, and Marcus Aurelius’ readiness to be corrected, express the same insight.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “They are abundant, O king, that can always speak agreeable words. The speaker, however, is rare, as also the hearer, of words that are disagreeable but medicinal.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells King Dhritarashtra that flatterers are everywhere, but people who speak or accept bitter-but-healing truth are rare.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘Disagreeable but medicinal’ words are exactly the Kural’s ear-bittering speech that a great king must bear.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva 37 (Vidura Niti), tr. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match, addressed to a king.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs says a fool hates correction, but a wise person loves the one who corrects him.
christianity.tie_back: The wise ruler of the Kural is the ‘wise man’ who welcomes rebuke rather than resenting it.
christianity._accuracy_note: General wisdom teaching; not specific to kings.

islam.quote_or_event: “The best fighting (jihad) in the path of Allah is (to speak) a word of justice to an oppressive ruler.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet said one of the greatest acts of striving is to tell a truth to an unjust ruler’s face.
islam.tie_back: Presents the other side of the Kural’s relationship: speaking hard truth to power is a sacred duty, which the good king must bear.
islam._accuracy_note: Speaker’s perspective rather than the ruler’s; complementary match.

judaism.quote_or_event: The prophet Nathan confronts King David with the parable of the poor man’s lamb and declares “Thou art the man”; David, rather than punishing him, answers “I have sinned against the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: When the prophet Nathan boldly accused King David of a terrible wrong, David accepted the rebuke instead of getting angry.
judaism.tie_back: A king who bears words bitter to the ear — the exact virtue this kural praises.
judaism._accuracy_note: Narrative match; the short phrases are KJV wording but the entry summarises the episode.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says someone who points out your faults is as valuable as a guide to buried treasure.
buddhism.tie_back: Reproof as treasure — the reason the Kural’s king should bear bitter words.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match; addressed to all, not specifically rulers.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Nestor tells Agamemnon that because Zeus has given him the sceptre and the right to judge, it is his duty above all to speak and also to listen, and to act on another man’s good counsel — urging him to repair his quarrel with Achilles.
greek_mythology.explanation: The wise old Nestor reminds King Agamemnon that a king must listen to advice, even advice he does not want to hear.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The duty of a sceptred king to hear hard counsel is the Kural’s central point.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If any man is able to convince me and show me that I do not think or act right, I will gladly change. For I seek the truth by which no man was ever injured.”
philosophy.explanation: The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius writes that he will gladly change if anyone shows him he is wrong.
philosophy.tie_back: A ruling emperor embracing correction — the Kural’s king who bears bitter words.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match from an actual ruler’s private reflections.

kurals.tamil:
கொடையளி செங்கோல் குடியோம்பல் நான்கும்
உடையானாம் வேந்தர்க் கொளி.
kurals.transliteration:
Kodaiyali sengol kudiyombal naangum
Udaiyaanaam vendhark koli.
kurals.meaning: The one who has these four — generosity, compassion, a just sceptre, and care for his people — is the light among kings.
kurals.elementary: In a dark room, a lamp helps everyone see. This kural says the best king is like a lamp for all other kings, because he gives generously, is kind, rules fairly, and takes care of his people.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with a second set of four, this time outward-facing: kodai (gifts), ali (grace or compassion), sengol (the ‘straight sceptre’, i.e., just rule), and kudi ombal (nurturing the people). Where 382 described the king’s inner capacities, this kural describes their effects on subjects, and it crowns the one who has them as oli — the lamp or radiance — of kings, a model by which other rulers are measured. The sengol (straight sceptre) is a central symbol of Tamil political thought, contrasted with the kodungol (crooked sceptre) of the tyrant in later chapters. The image of the just ruler as light recurs in David’s last words in 2 Samuel, and the Hebrew Bible’s ‘sceptre of righteousness’ offers a remarkably close verbal parallel.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kalidasa says King Dilipa was the true father of his subjects, because he educated, protected, and sustained them, while their own fathers were merely the cause of their birth.
hinduism.explanation: A Sanskrit poem praises a king who cared for his people so completely that he was more of a father to them than their real fathers.
hinduism.tie_back: Embodies kudi ombal (nurturing the people) and ali (compassion), the heart of the Kural’s ‘light of kings’.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong on care and protection, generosity implied.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: a sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of thy kingdom.”
christianity.explanation: The Letter to the Hebrews describes Christ’s kingdom as ruled by a ‘sceptre of righteousness’.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Sceptre of righteousness’ is almost a word-for-word equivalent of the Kural’s sengol (the straight sceptre).
christianity._accuracy_note: Striking verbal match for the just sceptre; the other three qualities not listed.

islam.quote_or_event: “The Imam (ruler) is the guardian of his subjects and is responsible for them.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that a ruler is like a shepherd who must answer for how he cared for his people.
islam.tie_back: Matches kudi ombal — the ruler’s duty to nurture and protect the people.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on care for subjects; generosity and compassion implicit.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God. And he shall be as the light of the morning, when the sun riseth, even a morning without clouds;”
judaism.explanation: In his last words, King David says a just ruler is like the light of a clear sunrise.
judaism.tie_back: Just rule producing radiance — the same image as the Kural’s ‘light of kings’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on justice and the light metaphor.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta, the wheel-turning monarch is told to rely on the Dhamma, provide protection for all his people, allow no crime in his realm, and give wealth to the poor; a later king’s failure to give to the needy sets off a spiral of theft and violence (DN 26).
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells of an ideal king who protects everyone and gives to the poor; when a later king stops giving, crime spreads and society collapses.
buddhism.tie_back: Combines generosity, just rule, and protection of the people — the Kural’s four qualities of the model king.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; close match to all four elements.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...like that of some blameless king, who upholds righteousness, as the monarch over a great and valiant nation: the earth yields its wheat and barley, the trees are loaded with fruit, the ewes bring forth lambs, and the sea abounds with fish by reason of his virtues, and his people do good deeds under him.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus compares Penelope’s fame to that of a just king, under whose rule the land flourishes and the people do good.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The just king whose virtue nourishes his whole people is the Greek image of the Kural’s ‘light of kings’.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on just rule and people’s welfare.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...there is no one in any rule who, in so far as he is a ruler, considers or enjoins what is for his own interest, but always what is for the interest of his subject or suitable to his art;”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues that a true ruler always acts for the good of those he rules, not for himself.
philosophy.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s ideal of the king defined by care for his people (kudi ombal).
philosophy._accuracy_note: Captures the ruler-for-subjects principle; not a list of the four virtues.
